content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, Led Zeppelin is widely considered to be one of the most influential and important rock bands of all time. The instrumentation for Led Zeppelin includes Jimmy Page on guitar, John Bonham on drums, John Paul Jones on bass and keyboards, and Robert Plant on lead vocals. Page's guitar work is especially noteworthy for its innovative use of distortion and effects, which create a dense and powerful sound that was not commonly heard in rock music at the time. Bonham's drumming style is also a key component of the band's sound, with his heavy and intricate rhythms standing out on many tracks. In terms of the lyrics, Led Zeppelin's songs often explore themes of mythology, love and heartbreak, and the supernatural. Plant's high-pitched wailing vocals also contributed to the band's unique sound and helped to convey the emotions present in their lyrics. Their songs frequently alluded to folklore and the occult, which adds to the mysterious atmosphere of their music. The lyrical themes present in Led Zeppelin's music resonate with fans for a variety of reasons. Many fans are drawn to the band's exploration of mythology and the supernatural, while others appreciate the emotional depth of their music. Led Zeppelin's music speaks to a wide range of listeners, as their blend of blues, hard rock, and folk continues to captivate audiences to this day. Some standout tracks from Led Zeppelin include "Stairway to Heaven," "Kashmir," and "Whole Lotta Love," all of which showcase the band's unique instrumentation and lyrics. In terms of live performances, Led Zeppelin was famous for their explosive and dynamic shows. They were known for their improvisational style, and their live performances often featured extended jams and solos. content:Speaker user says: How did the researchers create a 3D model of a rock art tableau from existing photographs, and why was this important for the project?: This week we meet up with Elizabeth Galvin, a curator at the British Museum, as she tells us about the African Rock Art Image Project and a beautiful piece of rock art in Zimbabwe.
The African Rock Art Image Project is documenting, researching and disseminating c. 25,000 digital images of rock art from throughout Africa. As an entirely digital collection, the project is exploring new ways that the audience interacts with and explores Africa’s rock art whilst it remains in situ. This model, from one site in Zimbabwe, was made from roughly 50 existing photographs from the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s (originally photographed by the Trust for African Rock Art) stitched together and annotated by project researchers.
As these photos were not purposefully taken for 3D modelling, they presented a unique challenge to making sure it was an accurate representation of the site. A key aim of our project is increasing access to this collection online, worldwide. However, with limited resources, we cannot always get out into the field to take new photographs. By creating 3D models, it gives perspective into some of the world’s oldest art that cannot be communicated solely through photos and allows visitors to understand more about the rock art of Africa and the people that made it.
This model is made from existing photographs of the Zombapata Cave in Mashonaland, Zimbabwe. The tableau is over 80 feet long and includes paintings of zebra, sheep, sable antelope, bee’s nests, lions, a large troupe of baboons and animal footprints. A large yellow elephant dominates the scene and several kudu (antelope) are scattered throughout. Both elephants and kudu had significant meaning to the San|Bushmen people of this area, as demonstrated by their reoccurrence in rock art in Zimbabwe.
Most rock art in southern Africa was made by the ancestors of today’s San|Bushmen people. San|Bushmen is a collective term used to describe the many different hunter-gatherer-fisher groups living in this area with related languages and cultural traditions. The oldest scientifically dated rock art in the southern Africa is c.30,000 years old. The rock art images they left behind reveal insight into their lives, survival and spiritual beliefs over thousands of years.
European invasion and settlement of southern Africa from the 1650s onwards had a devastating impact on the San|Bushmen’s traditional nomadic lifestyle. New diseases, wars and enclosing of lands greatly reduced their population and resulted in the loss of many traditions, including rock art (which has not been practiced for about 100 years). Few objects of the ancestors of the San|Bushmen survive that offer the same amount of insight into their world as rock art.
Through 3D modelling we are able to preserve, explore and disseminate some of the world’s oldest art.
The African Rock Art Image Project is supported by the Arcadia Fund.

content:Speaker assistant says: I recently had the chance to play the board game "Pandemic." Pandemic is a cooperative game in which players must work together to fight and cure four major diseases that are spreading across the world. The mechanics of the game are fairly simple, but the level of strategy involved is quite high.

At the start of the game, players are each given a role with unique abilities that will aid in fighting the diseases. Players take turns moving around the board, treating infected cities, and building research stations. Along the way, they must also collect cards that correspond to the four diseases, which they can later use to cure those diseases. 

One of the most unique features of Pandemic is the way the diseases spread across the board. As the game progresses, new cities become infected, and outbreaks occur when too many infected cities are adjacent to one another. This creates a sense of urgency and makes it imperative that players work quickly and efficiently. 

Overall, I found the game to be incredibly challenging and engaging. The level of strategy involved is high, and players must work together effectively in order to win. The game also has a high replayability value, as the infections are randomized each time the game is played. 

The components of the game are of high quality, with sturdy game pieces and an attractive game board. The artwork is colorful and detailed, adding to the overall experience of playing the game. 

In conclusion, I would highly recommend Pandemic to anyone who enjoys strategy and cooperative games. content:Speaker user says: Here is a piece of text: Actor Paul Wegman, who shone as brightly on local stages in the roles of William Shakespeare as he did playing the drag queen Miss P, died early Tuesday of complications resulting from AIDS. He was 60.
Wegman lived two lives onstage -- the first as one of the busiest and most beloved actors in Orlando theater, one who could turn himself into anything from a dissipated old geezer in an offbeat Sam Shepard drama to a giddy Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.
The second was as a character he created, once described as "the most famous drag queen in the Southeast" -- the sharp, spiky Miss P, who insulted unwitting audience members from the stage at the Parliament House for 25 years.
"There was always Paul, and then there was P at the Parliament House," said Mark Edward Smith, a friend and fellow actor. "To me, they were never the same people."
When Wegman was playing Miss P, people called him fierce and fearless.
"She had her own personality -- abrasive, incredibly quick-witted and beautiful," said Julia Gagne, a theater professor at Valencia Community College and a longtime friend. "You didn't want to be on her bad side."
But offstage Wegman had little in common with the fearsome Miss P -- except, as Smith said, "he was one of the most fearless people I know." The private Wegman could be difficult, his friends say, but he was also funny, generous and kind.
"He was such a prickly character," said actress Pam Baumann, who knew Wegman as a director but also became a good friend. "You had to know him to know this was a joke. When you got to know him, he was a warm fuzzy. He was such fun to be with. That wonderful enthusiasm for everything just sucked everybody in."
Wegman grew up in Rochester, N.Y., where he was an overweight child who listened to Broadway musicals and would sing and dance in his room.
"The theater was his salvation," Gagne said.
After graduating from high school, he left Rochester and was working for a carnival when he moved to Orlando around 1965.
In those days, "Orlando's gay scene was quiet and reserved," wrote James T. Sears, a historian who has chronicled gay and lesbian life in the South. Wegman first began to play Miss P in the early 1970s at a place called the Palace Club, near the Orlando Executive Airport, where Sears described him as "the boy with strawberry hair."
In 1975 he moved his act to the Parliament House Motor Inn on seedy Orange Blossom Trail, where new owners were fashioning a gay resort. There, Wegman could do what he liked -- not only playing Miss P, who acted as emcee to the other drag queens, but also staging an all-male version of A Chorus Line and eventually presenting a number of gay-themed plays.
Miss P became known not so much for her Broadway ballads but for the way she played to and insulted the audience.
"He would turn up the house lights and pick on people," said Margaret Nolan, who worked with him at several Orlando theaters. "He would go right out there to them, get right up in their faces. People came there for this. Being insulted by Miss P was a kind of honor."
And even if you didn't like drag, Smith said, Wegman was amazing.
"He was just brilliant in talking to the audience and working the audience. He was just a brilliant improvisational comedian.
"One night he had on a dress with a huge butterfly on it. The butterfly fell off, and he proceeded to do 20 minutes on that butterfly. I was crying on the floor, it was so funny. The fact that he was in a dress was incidental."
That skill at improvisation came from a keen intelligence. He read incessantly, and he never stopped preparing for roles he was to play.
"He'd get excited," Baumann said. "He'd continue to study the play, and he'd continue to find things. He didn't quit. He was always perfecting what he was supposed to be."
Wegman studied theater under Sara Daspin at Seminole Community College in the late 1970s or early 1980s, and there he began to be known as a serious actor, playing such roles as John Merrick, the hideously deformed central character in The Elephant Man and the conflicted Rev. Hale in The Crucible.
He also began to direct, at SCC, Valencia Community College and various community and alternative theaters in the area.
"The way he directed is perfect for educational theater," said Gagne. "He was able to ask the right questions."
"I always said I went to the Paul Wegman School of Acting," Baumann said. "He taught me so much."
As an actor, he began to take on the widest imaginable variety of roles -- the grizzled old Dodge in Sam Shepard's Buried Child; the imperious Lady Bracknell in The Importance of Being Earnest; Scrooge in at least four different productions of A Christmas Carol and a whole slew of Shakespearean characters, including a humorously humorless Malvolio in Twelfth Night and the sorcerer Prospero in two wildly different productions of The Tempest.

content:Speaker user says: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: Who was Miss P and how did she become a popular character in Orlando's drag scene?

Passage: Actor Paul Wegman, who shone as brightly on local stages in the roles of William Shakespeare as he did playing the drag queen Miss P, died early Tuesday of complications resulting from AIDS. He was 60.
Wegman lived two lives onstage -- the first as one of the busiest and most beloved actors in Orlando theater, one who could turn himself into anything from a dissipated old geezer in an offbeat Sam Shepard drama to a giddy Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.
The second was as a character he created, once described as "the most famous drag queen in the Southeast" -- the sharp, spiky Miss P, who insulted unwitting audience members from the stage at the Parliament House for 25 years.
"There was always Paul, and then there was P at the Parliament House," said Mark Edward Smith, a friend and fellow actor. "To me, they were never the same people."
When Wegman was playing Miss P, people called him fierce and fearless.
"She had her own personality -- abrasive, incredibly quick-witted and beautiful," said Julia Gagne, a theater professor at Valencia Community College and a longtime friend. "You didn't want to be on her bad side."
But offstage Wegman had little in common with the fearsome Miss P -- except, as Smith said, "he was one of the most fearless people I know." The private Wegman could be difficult, his friends say, but he was also funny, generous and kind.
"He was such a prickly character," said actress Pam Baumann, who knew Wegman as a director but also became a good friend. "You had to know him to know this was a joke. When you got to know him, he was a warm fuzzy. He was such fun to be with. That wonderful enthusiasm for everything just sucked everybody in."
Wegman grew up in Rochester, N.Y., where he was an overweight child who listened to Broadway musicals and would sing and dance in his room.
"The theater was his salvation," Gagne said.
After graduating from high school, he left Rochester and was working for a carnival when he moved to Orlando around 1965.
In those days, "Orlando's gay scene was quiet and reserved," wrote James T. Sears, a historian who has chronicled gay and lesbian life in the South. Wegman first began to play Miss P in the early 1970s at a place called the Palace Club, near the Orlando Executive Airport, where Sears described him as "the boy with strawberry hair."
In 1975 he moved his act to the Parliament House Motor Inn on seedy Orange Blossom Trail, where new owners were fashioning a gay resort. There, Wegman could do what he liked -- not only playing Miss P, who acted as emcee to the other drag queens, but also staging an all-male version of A Chorus Line and eventually presenting a number of gay-themed plays.
Miss P became known not so much for her Broadway ballads but for the way she played to and insulted the audience.
"He would turn up the house lights and pick on people," said Margaret Nolan, who worked with him at several Orlando theaters. "He would go right out there to them, get right up in their faces. People came there for this. Being insulted by Miss P was a kind of honor."
And even if you didn't like drag, Smith said, Wegman was amazing.
"He was just brilliant in talking to the audience and working the audience. He was just a brilliant improvisational comedian.
"One night he had on a dress with a huge butterfly on it. The butterfly fell off, and he proceeded to do 20 minutes on that butterfly. I was crying on the floor, it was so funny. The fact that he was in a dress was incidental."
That skill at improvisation came from a keen intelligence. He read incessantly, and he never stopped preparing for roles he was to play.
"He'd get excited," Baumann said. "He'd continue to study the play, and he'd continue to find things. He didn't quit. He was always perfecting what he was supposed to be."
Wegman studied theater under Sara Daspin at Seminole Community College in the late 1970s or early 1980s, and there he began to be known as a serious actor, playing such roles as John Merrick, the hideously deformed central character in The Elephant Man and the conflicted Rev. Hale in The Crucible.
He also began to direct, at SCC, Valencia Community College and various community and alternative theaters in the area.
"The way he directed is perfect for educational theater," said Gagne. "He was able to ask the right questions."
"I always said I went to the Paul Wegman School of Acting," Baumann said. "He taught me so much."
As an actor, he began to take on the widest imaginable variety of roles -- the grizzled old Dodge in Sam Shepard's Buried Child; the imperious Lady Bracknell in The Importance of Being Earnest; Scrooge in at least four different productions of A Christmas Carol and a whole slew of Shakespearean characters, including a humorously humorless Malvolio in Twelfth Night and the sorcerer Prospero in two wildly different productions of The Tempest.
"Some people are just born to be onstage and to channel characters," said Nolan. "He had a playfulness about him all the time -- an intellectual playfulness, even as Miss P."
In fact, you couldn't take your eyes off him.
"He has whatever that quality is that really makes you want to watch someone -- whether you call it charisma or presence," Gagne said. "There was just nothing he couldn't do."

An Integrated Bayesian Approach for Effective Multi-Truth Discovery. Xianzhi Wang, Quan Z. Sheng, Xiu Susie Fang, Lina Yao, Xiaofei Xu, and Xue Li.
Truth-finding is the fundamental technique for corroborating reports from multiple sources in both data integration and collective intelligent applications. Traditional truth-finding methods assume a single true value for each data item and therefore cannot deal will multiple true values (i.e., the multi-truth-finding problem). So far, the existing approaches handle the multi-truth-finding problem in the same way as single-truth-finding problems. Unfortunately, the multi-truth-finding problem has its unique features, such as the involvement of sets of values in claims, different implications of inter-value mutual exclusion, and larger source proflles. Considering these features could provide new opportunities for obtaining more accurate truth-finding results. Based on this insight, we propose an integrated Bayesian approach to the multi-truth-finding problem, by taking these features into account. To improve the truth-finding efficiency, we reformulate the multi-truth-finding problem model based on the mappings between sources and (sets of) values. New mutual exclusive relations are defined to reflect the possible co-existence of multiple true values. A finer-grained copy detection method is also proposed to deal with sources with large profiles. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show the effectiveness of our approach.
